slides.title: Le Chatelier's principle
slides.sub: What actually happens when you disturb an equilibrium — in 5 slides.

slides.heading: The idea
slides.text: Disturb a system at equilibrium and it shifts to **partly oppose** the change. Partly — never fully. It settles at a new equilibrium, not back at the old one.

slides.heading: The example
slides.text: Four moles of gas become two, and the forward reaction is exothermic. Both of those matter for everything that follows.

slides.heading: Three ways to disturb it
items: **Add $\ce{N2}$ or $\ce{H2}$** — shifts right, consuming what you added.
**Raise the pressure** — shifts right, toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
**Raise the temperature** — shifts left, away from the exothermic direction.

slides.heading: The part that's easy to miss
slides.text: Concentration and pressure move the **position** of equilibrium, but $K_c$ stays fixed — the ratio rebalances back to it. **Only temperature changes $K_c$.**

slides.heading: Why the Haber process is a compromise
slides.text: High pressure helps yield, so industry pushes it hard. High temperature **hurts** yield — but a cold reactor is uselessly slow. So it runs hot enough to be fast and accepts the lower yield: roughly $450\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $200\ \mathrm{atm}$.
